title: Lazarus Saturday
hook: the Orthodox celebrate Lazarus raised, the day before Palm Sunday

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mothering Sunday: a day to visit the mother church, and your mother. Your line was go home. Where did home turn out to be? Day one thousand twenty-seven.

A message reaches Jesus from two sisters in Bethany, Mary and Martha. In the King James Bible it's one line: "Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick." Their brother Lazarus. And Jesus waits. He stays where he is two more days. By the time he reaches Bethany, Lazarus has been in the grave four days. Martha comes out to meet him on the road, and later Mary falls at his feet, and each of them says the same sentence: if you had been here, my brother would not have died. Then Jesus stands in front of a cave with a stone across it and asks for the stone to be rolled away. Martha, practical to the end, warns him about the smell. On the Saturday before Palm Sunday, Orthodox Christians tell this whole story again. Today, Lazarus Saturday.

John tells this one slowly, and three short lines carry it. The first is two words long: "Jesus wept." He stands with the sisters at the grave, and he weeps. John doesn't skip the grief to hurry on to the miracle, and neither does Jesus. The second line is a shout. In the King James: "Lazarus, come forth." And the dead man comes out, still bound hand and foot in grave clothes, his face wrapped in a cloth. The third line is easy to miss. Jesus turns to the people standing around and says: "Loose him, and let him go." Notice who does what. Jesus calls him out. Everyone else has to do the unwrapping. In this story, coming back takes a voice, and then a lot of ordinary hands working at knots. Now, why keep it on this particular Saturday? Because John sets the two scenes side by side. Right after Bethany, he says, a crowd that had heard about Lazarus took palm branches and went out to meet Jesus on the road into Jerusalem. So Orthodox churches treat this day as a hinge between Lent and Holy Week. They hear it as a preview of Easter: the one who calls his friend out of a tomb is about to walk toward his own. And John adds a hard detail. After the raising, the chief priests talk about putting Lazarus to death as well. Being called out of the grave didn't make his life safe. It made it visible.

Here's the practice: remember a friend who was restored. Someone who came back from something. An illness, a dark year, a long silence, a habit that nearly had them. Settle, and breathe. Bring their face to mind, the way it looked at the worst point, and the way it looks now. Then think about the hands. Who helped unwrap them? Maybe you were one of those hands. Maybe you only watched from a distance. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name. If you don't, simply hold them in mind, glad they came out. The bell holds the time.
Lazarus Saturday. The day before Palm Sunday, when Orthodox Christians remember Jesus calling his friend out of the tomb at Bethany.
Your line: come out. Today, send one message to someone who's gone quiet for a long time, even if it only says their name. Day one thousand twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Orthodox Christians keep Lazarus Saturday the day before Palm Sunday, with a service that retells John 11 and, in some places, by making palm crosses or special breads for the next day.

fork.setup: you're Martha. Jesus is standing at your brother's tomb, four days too late, and he asks for the stone to be rolled away. what do you say?
options: Lord, by this time he stinketh: for he hath been dead four days.
fork.reveal: practical Martha warns him about the smell. Jesus answers that if she believes she will see the glory of God, and the stone is moved.

original.note: Greek: here, out! — the call in John 11:43, translated "come forth."

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle story where a dead man walks out.
what it means: a friend who weeps first, calls second, and leaves the unwrapping to everyone standing around.
what a scholar hears: John sets this sign just before the palm-branch crowd, and right after it the chief priests plan to kill Lazarus too (John 12:10).
